voiceover.text: Here are the three systems, each with an empty fuel gauge. Food fills them, but not equally. Two athletes at one club eat the same meals. One's a fifteen-hundred-metre runner who trains hard for ninety minutes most days. The other's a shot putter, whose ninety minutes hold maybe two minutes of maximal effort. One of them is eating badly for their sport. Which one? And the runner takes iron, and says it gives them energy. But iron has no kilojoules at all. So how could it help?

Nutrition is the supply chain for those fuels. You met the three macronutrients in digestion: carbohydrate in a small glycogen store, fat in a huge store, and protein for building and repair. What's new is which system each one feeds. Carbohydrate is the only food fuel the body can use without oxygen, so it feeds glycolysis and the aerobic system. Fat feeds only the aerobic system. And protein has no fuel store, so it adds only a small share of exercise energy.

From last time, intensity decides the mix. At rest, fat supplies most of the energy. At about sixty-five per cent of maximum effort, the two are roughly equal. That's the crossover. Above about eighty-five per cent of maximum effort, carbohydrate supplies most of it. Now the puzzle. The runner spends long stretches above the crossover, so most of their energy comes from a store that lasts about ninety minutes. Carbohydrate decides whether they finish the session. The shot putter's efforts last seconds, run on phosphocreatine, and cost little in total. Their priority is protein, to build muscle. So the same meals can't suit both, and it's the runner who's short-changed.

So how much does an active person need? Guidelines are written per kilogram of body mass per day, because a bigger body needs more of the same things. And carbohydrate tracks training load: about three to five grams per kilogram for light training, and six to ten for heavy endurance work. Take a sixty-kilogram netballer in light training. Three to five, times sixty, is one hundred and eighty to three hundred grams. A ninety-five-kilogram rower in heavy training: six to ten, times ninety-five, is five hundred and seventy to nine hundred and fifty grams. On the same diet, the netballer is covered, and the rower gets about a third of what they need.

Protein rises from about one point two grams per kilogram to about two in heavy training. But two is roughly a ceiling. Beyond it, the extra isn't stored as muscle. It's burned, or stored as fat. The training is the signal to grow, and protein is the material. Fat works the other way. It has a floor, about twenty to thirty-five per cent of energy, and rarely below twenty. Too little, and the body can't absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, or make some hormones well. Very low intakes can also lead to low energy availability, which you met earlier.

scenes.title: iron: no energy, but a limit removed

voiceover.text: Now the iron puzzle. Micronutrients, the vitamins and minerals we need in tiny amounts, carry no energy. They're part of the machinery that releases it. Iron sits at the centre of haemoglobin, and of myoglobin in muscle. It's what oxygen binds to. Without enough iron, less oxygen reaches the mitochondria, so the aerobic system is capped lower. At the same pace, more energy has to come from the anaerobic systems, and fatigue comes sooner. So iron doesn't give energy. It removes a limit. But only if you're short of it. Extra iron gives a well-stocked athlete nothing, and too much does harm. A blood test decides, not a label.

You met these micronutrients in digestion. Here's how each one can limit performance. B group vitamins are coenzymes, helpers the enzymes need. Calcium triggers every contraction and builds bone, but a low intake shows up mainly in the bones, as a higher risk of stress fractures. Vitamin C helps you absorb iron, and with vitamin E it limits damage from heavy training. And sodium and potassium, lost in sweat, let nerves and muscle fibres fire.

Last, water. It has no energy, but running short hurts performance fastest. As you saw with the delivery chain, sweat shrinks the plasma, so stroke volume falls, heart rate climbs, and less blood reaches the skin, so core temperature rises. Losing about two per cent of body mass, that's one point four kilograms for a seventy-kilogram athlete, measurably cuts endurance and decision-making. In team sport, a skill error can be an early sign. What to drink, and when, comes later.
Two things to remember. Macronutrients are the fuel, and micronutrients are the machinery. And correcting a deficiency helps, but exceeding a requirement doesn't.

Two exam questions. First. A fifty-kilogram swimmer moves from light training to heavy endurance training. Calculate her daily carbohydrate range before and after, and explain why it changes. Pause here to answer.

Light: three to five, times fifty, is one hundred and fifty to two hundred and fifty grams. Heavy: six to ten, times fifty, is three hundred to five hundred. Her mass hasn't changed. Her training has. More work above the crossover empties more glycogen. The classic mistake is saying requirements depend on body size alone.

Second. A runner's intake of B group vitamins is very low. Explain how this could reduce performance, even though B vitamins supply no energy, and whether a runner with normal levels would gain from taking extra. Pause here to answer.

B vitamins are coenzymes in glycolysis and aerobic metabolism. Short of them, those enzymes work more slowly, so ATP is rebuilt more slowly even with plenty of fuel, and fatigue comes sooner. Correcting the shortage helps. A runner with normal levels gains nothing. The classic mistake is saying vitamins give you energy.

So, to judge any diet, match the fuel to the work, then check the machinery. Now turn this graph around. If intensity decides the fuel, then the intensity a coach chooses decides which system gets trained. So what makes a session aerobic or anaerobic?
